sentenceSets.sentence: Advances in cartography during the Age of Exploration transformed European understanding of the world's geography.

answerChoices.reasoning: Navigation is the practice of getting a ship where it is meant to go, but the sentence credits these advances with changing what Europeans understood about the shape of the world, which is a matter of representation rather than steering.
Surveying takes measurements on the ground, whereas the transformation described is in a picture of the whole world, assembled far from the places measured.
Astronomy studies the heavens, and the object transformed here is explicitly the understanding of the world's geography.
Geodesy is the determination of the earth's precise size and shape, a narrow mathematical problem that does not by itself remake how a continent pictures the rest of the globe.
Better hulls made the voyages possible, but the sentence attributes the change in understanding to the advance itself, not to the vessels that carried anyone.
Printing spread whatever was already known more widely, while the sentence describes a transformation in the understanding itself.
Diplomacy concerns relations between states, which is unrelated to a changed grasp of world geography.
Weather prediction was vital at sea, yet the knowledge said to be transformed here is of where places are, not of what the sky will do.
Mythology is the body of traditional stories a culture tells, the very thing that accurate knowledge of the world displaces.
The raising of crops and livestock has no connection to European understanding of world geography.
Preserving animal specimens belongs to an entirely different field from the one the sentence describes.

sentenceSets.sentence: Modern cartography depends less on the surveyor's chain than on satellite imagery, yet the decisions about which borders to draw and whose place names to print remain as political as ever.

answerChoices.reasoning: Topography is a feature of the land itself, something that exists whether or not anyone records it, while the sentence describes a practice whose practitioners make choices about borders and names.
Photogrammetry is the technique of extracting measurements from images, so it names one of the tools the sentence contrasts, not the wider craft in which political choices are made.
Reconnaissance is the gathering of information about terrain, but the political weight here attaches to what gets printed on the finished product.
Demography counts populations, whereas the disputed decisions listed are about border lines and place names on a map.
Satellite imagery is used for spying too, but the sentence names a practice whose output carries printed place names, which secret intelligence does not publish.
Archaeology reconstructs the past from material remains, and the contested items here are current borders and the names attached to living places.
Telemetry is the transmission of measurements from a distance and has no stake in which name for a city appears in print.
Urbanism concerns how cities are planned and lived in, not the drawing of national boundaries that the sentence calls political.
Alchemy has no connection to satellites, surveyors' chains, or borders.
The arrangement of dance has nothing to do with the practice the sentence contrasts with surveying.
Throwing one's voice belongs to an unrelated field entirely.

sentenceSets.sentence: She gave up poetry for cartography after a summer of tracing the glacier's retreat, line by faint line, onto sheets of gridded paper.

answerChoices.reasoning: A glaciologist studies why the ice is retreating, but the summer described is spent transferring its edges onto gridded sheets, which is an exercise in recording position rather than explaining cause.
Draftsmanship names the manual skill of drawing precisely, and the sentence describes her taking up a field of work, not merely acquiring a technique.
Geology concerns rock and the earth's structure, whereas what she records is the shifting outline of the ice from one season to the next.
Surveillance implies watching people, and the object of her attention is a glacier whose successive edges she is putting onto paper.
Calligraphy is the beautiful shaping of letters, but she is tracing the retreating margin of a glacier onto a grid, not writing.
Climatology studies long-run patterns in the atmosphere, while the faint lines she draws record the position of the ice itself on the ground.
Mountaineering is the climbing itself, whereas the sentence dwells on the paper and the lines drawn on it.
Botany studies plants, which never appear in a description devoted to ice margins and gridded sheets.
Bookkeeping has no plausible link to a summer spent outdoors tracing a glacier.
Sculpture works in three dimensions and would not be practiced on sheets of gridded paper.
Dentistry is wholly unrelated to anything the sentence describes.
